name: Progressive muscle relaxation (PMR)
evidenceLevel: Supportive as a component skill. NICE CG113 lists applied relaxation, which is built on PMR, as a high-intensity psychological option for GAD alongside CBT. A 2008 meta-analysis (Manzoni et al.) found relaxation training reduced anxiety across studies. NCCIH describes relaxation techniques as generally safe but notes limited evidence for specific conditions. In panic CBT packages, a 2018 component network meta-analysis (Pompoli et al.) linked muscle relaxation with lower efficacy, so PMR is not a first-choice component for panic.
purpose: Teaches the client to notice the contrast between tense and relaxed muscles by tightening and then releasing muscle groups in a set order. It lowers physical tension linked to worry and gives the client a portable self-calming skill. PMR is also the first stage of applied relaxation. Use it as one skill within a broader treatment plan, not as a stand-alone treatment for an anxiety condition.
steps: Explain the rationale in plain terms: worry often shows up as muscle tension, and the client can learn to spot and release it. Before starting, ask about pain, injuries, recent surgery, pregnancy, and heart, blood-pressure, back, neck or joint problems.
Agree on a 0-10 tension scale (0 = fully relaxed, 10 = most tense) and take a rating before the exercise.

Set up the position: seated with feet flat on the floor, or lying down. Eyes may be closed or resting on one spot. Offer the eyes-open option by default to clients with a trauma history or anyone who prefers it.
Model one cycle: tighten a muscle group for about 5 seconds at moderate effort (never to the point of pain), release all at once, then rest for 15 to 20 seconds while noticing the change.

Guide the client through the 12 groups in the order used on the pmr-homework handout: hands, upper arms, forehead, eyes and nose, mouth and jaw, neck, shoulders, upper back, belly, hips, upper legs, lower legs and feet. Use a slow, steady voice and leave silence during the rest periods.
Skip or only lightly tense any area with pain or injury. Watch for distress (breath-holding, tearfulness, startle, a glazed look) and pause or switch to eyes-open grounding if it appears.
Close with a few slow breaths, a brief head-to-toe scan, and a gradual return: count from 1 to 5, wiggle fingers and toes, open eyes, and stand slowly.
Take a second tension rating. Ask what the client noticed, including any discomfort or anxiety that came up while relaxing, and normalize it.

Assign daily home practice with the pmr-homework handout and its log. Once the client is fluent (often after one to two weeks of daily practice), shorten the routine by combining groups (arms, face, shoulders and belly, legs).
script: We are going to practice a skill that helps your body let go of tension. You will tighten a group of muscles, hold for a few seconds, and then let go.
Tighten firmly, but never so hard that it hurts. If a part of your body has pain or an injury, skip it or tighten it just a little.
You can close your eyes or rest them on one spot in front of you. Choose whatever feels best.
Let's start with your hands. Make two fists. Squeeze... hold it... and now let go. Let your fingers go loose.
Notice the difference between tight and loose. There is nothing you need to do. Just notice.
Now your upper arms. Bend your elbows and tighten these muscles. Hold... and let go. Let your arms drop and rest.
We will keep moving through your body the same way: tighten, hold, let go, and notice.
If your mind wanders, that is okay. Gently bring your attention back to your muscles.
Now take a slow breath. I will count from 1 to 5. When I reach 5, open your eyes and sit up slowly.
How did that feel? Some people feel calm. Some feel a bit strange or even nervous the first few times. Both are common, and it tends to get easier with practice.
contraindications: Medical cautions: pain, injuries, recent surgery, pregnancy, and heart, blood-pressure, back, neck or joint problems. Skip or lightly tense affected areas, and suggest the client check with their medical provider if unsure.
Muscle cramps: if a cramp occurs, stop tensing that group and stretch gently. Use less effort for that area next time.

Relaxation-induced anxiety: some clients feel more anxious as they relax (for example, a fear of losing control). Prepare them in advance, keep the first practice short, use eyes open, and frame the feeling as safe and temporary.

Trauma history or dissociation: NCCIH notes rare reports that relaxation techniques can worsen symptoms in people with a history of abuse or trauma, epilepsy, or certain psychiatric conditions. Offer eyes-open practice, let the client control the pace, and stop and switch to grounding if the client seems disconnected.
Not a stand-alone treatment for panic attacks. In panic CBT, muscle relaxation has been linked to weaker outcomes; prioritize interoceptive exposure and cognitive work for panic.
Not a crisis intervention. If the client reports thoughts of self-harm or harm to others, pause the exercise and follow your risk-assessment procedures.
Advise against practicing while driving or operating machinery.
culturalAdaptations: Ask how the client feels about closing their eyes, lying down, or relaxing deeply in front of a clinician. Offer seated and eyes-open versions by default.

Use plain, concrete names for body parts and check translations with a professional interpreter; some languages have no direct word for 'tension.' Let the client choose words that fit, such as 'tight,' 'heavy' or 'knotted.'
For clients who describe distress through the body (headaches, neck pain, 'nerves'), link PMR to the client's own explanation of the symptom rather than insisting on a psychological frame.
Adapt positions for disability, chronic pain, older age, or religious dress. PMR can be done fully clothed and seated, with no touch from the clinician.
If recordings are used for home practice, offer them in the client's preferred language and, where possible, in a voice the client finds calming.

faithIntegrated.note: If the client asks for it, they may pair each release with a short word, phrase, prayer or verse from their own tradition (for example, a word for peace or trust), or close the practice with a brief prayer they choose. The client picks the words and decides whether to use them. The clinician does not add religious content the client has not asked for.
faithIntegrated.consentNote: Offer only if the client raises faith or spirituality as a resource, and only after informed consent. Explain that the faith element is optional, that the standard version works without it, and that the client can change or stop it at any time. Use the client's own beliefs and words; never introduce or impose religious content. Record the consent discussion in your own clinical record, not in this app. See the AACC Code of Ethics on consent for spiritual interventions and the ACA Code of Ethics on informed consent and not imposing counselor values.
